sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Continual learning (CL) seeks to adapt pretrained models while preserving prior capabilities. Yet the tasks supplied for preservation cover only part of what a model knows, while forgetting can extend beyond them. Recent work shows that language models can supplement this limited evidence by generating useful replay without access to their original training data. This raises a question about self-preservation: can a model help choose preservation targets that protect its own capabilities more broadly? To study this question, we organize task descriptions and their examples into Task Banks, whose entries can be selected and combined to guide replay generation by a frozen model. Continual instruction tuning with Qwen models of varying sizes yields three findings. First, the new task and learning rate shape which prior capabilities degrade, while tracking previously correct answers reveals losses that average accuracy can conceal. Second, generated replay reduces forgetting on tasks outside the bank. Combining partial banks strengthens this protection, improving mean retention of previously correct answers over either bank alone across the tested sizes. Third, the model can also help choose replay targets: selection informed by the new task improves mean held-out retention over random selection at 4B, with similar new-task gains, although smaller models show no corresponding advantage. Under a fixed example budget, however, replacing new-task examples with replay improves preservation at the cost of smaller new-task gains. Together, these findings show that models can support broader self-preservation by generating replay data and, in some settings, choosing which tasks to replay.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Language models acquire broad capabilities through costly pretraining, yet need further training to incorporate new information or specialize in new domains. For these updates to produce cumulative improvement, models must learn new behavior without losing useful capabilities they already possess. Fine-tuning can instead degrade prior behavior, phenomenon known as catastrophic forgetting. Continual learning (CL) mitigates this problem through replay and updates constrained by evidence of prior behavior (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017; Chaudhry et al., 2019). When the original training data are unavailable, however, the tasks and examples supplied for preservation cover only part of what the model should retain (Cho et al., 2026a). Figure 1 illustrates this mismatch: new-task gains coexist with losses across prior tasks, and replay from real data reduces these losses without eliminating them. Recent work shows that language models can supplement limited preservation evidence via self-generated data (Sun et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2024; Marek et al., 2026). These findings motivate the idea of self-preservation: using models own knowledge to help retain its capabilities during adaptation. Generating more examples within supplied task can strengthen the evidence for that task, but does not by itself establish protection elsewhere. We therefore examine whether combining preservation targets improves retention beyond the supplied inventory, and whether information about the incoming task helps model select useful targets. To study these choices, we organize supplied preservation targets into Task Banks, compact collections of task descriptions and optional examples. Task-Bank Self-Replay uses frozen pre-update model to generate replay for selected entries and mixes these data with new-task examples during fine-tuning. The bank separates the specification of what to replay from the examples generated for it. Combining partial banks tests whether broader supplied coverage improves preservation. Within fixed bank, we compare random selection with model selection based on either the bank alone or the bank and information about the incoming task. These comparisons test the models contribution to choosing targets as well as generating replay data. Testing protection beyond the bank requires evaluation on behavior that did not guide replay construction. We reserve held-out tasks whose examples, labels, descriptions, and scores are excluded from bank construction and target selection. We also examine individual tasks and previously correct answers: gains on some tasks can offset losses on others, and newly corrected answers can offset losses of previously correct answers (Harmon et al., 2025). 1 Figure 1 Generated replay across supplied targets can protect held-out capabilities while retaining new-task gains. Top: prior-task accuracy changes. Bottom: incoming-task gains for Qwen3-0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B after one epoch on 1,024 MedQA examples at 1e-5. SFT uses incoming data only. Replay uses real prior-task examples and labels. Task-Bank Self-Replay uses model-generated questions and answers. Both replay methods cover MMLU, GSM8K, HellaSwag, and BoolQ. The plot shows seven prior tasks. Stars mark held-out tasks: ARC-C, WinoGrande, PIQA, and SVAMP. Points are five-seed means. Displayed error bars are 1 SE. The zero ring denotes pre-update accuracy, and all radial panels span 10 to +4 pp. Alongside task-level accuracy changes, we report Retention, the fraction of initially correct answers that remain correct after training, where paired predictions are available (Yang et al., 2026). We assess preservation together with new-task gains. Our instruction-tuning experiments span Qwen models from 0.6B to 4B (Yang et al., 2025) and yield three main findings: Training choices shape forgetting, and aggregate accuracy can conceal it. The incoming task and learning rate affect which prior capabilities degrade. Tracking individual tasks and previously correct answers reveals losses that favorable averages can hide. Generated replay supports preservation beyond its supplied targets. Task-Bank Self-Replay reduces held-out losses while retaining new-task gains. Combining two partial banks improves mean held-out Retention over either bank alone at all three tested Qwen3 sizes. The model can help choose useful replay targets. In the tested 4B setting, selection informed by the incoming task improves mean held-out Retention by 2.75 percentage points over random selection, with similar new-task gains. The same advantage does not appear at the smaller tested sizes.

sections.title: 2.1 Preservation Beyond Replay Targets
sections.content: Adapting to one task can change performance on others (Wang et al., 2023a). medical question-answering update, for example, changes both reasoning and commonsense performance in Figure 1. Gains on the incoming task do not tell us whether the model has retained its broader capabilities (Yang et al., 2026). We also evaluate prior tasks, including those absent from the data used to protect the model. Limited past data restrict the range of behavior represented in preservation evidence. Replaying retained examples supplies direct learning signal for their tasks (Chaudhry et al., 2019), while protection of other behavior depends on transfer. Generating more examples for the same targets adds depth to this evidence (Marek et al., 2026), but 2 does not by itself establish broader coverage. The amount of rehearsal and the choice of targets are therefore distinct design decisions. Task Banks record which behaviors the replay is intended to rehearse, without requiring complete inventory of the models capabilities. We use them to test whether different targets provide complementary protection and whether incoming-task information helps choose among them. We evaluate the bank-composition and target-selection comparisons on held-out tasks excluded from replay construction and selection. Performance on these tasks tests whether protection generalizes beyond the bank.

2.2 Task Banks
A Task Bank B = {b1, . . . , bm} contains compact task entries: a name, a description of the behavior and input/output
format, and optional demonstrations. Entries may describe overlapping skills. Replay can use one entry, a selected
subset S ⊆ {1, . . . , m}, or all supplied entries (the full bank). SFT uses incoming data only. Single-Task Replay
rehearses one supplied task. Replay uses stored examples and labels. Task-Bank Self-Replay instead obtains replay
answers from a frozen pre-update model.
sections.content: We select the entries to rehearse before generating replay. We compare random selection, selection using the bank alone, and selection also informed by the incoming task. The selector chooses entries, the frozen reference model generates replay, and the learner receives the update. These roles remain distinct even when they use the same checkpoint. Appendix C.6 specifies the selection inputs and prompts. Task-Bank Self-Replay generates its rehearsal data before the learner update. The endpoint, bank-composition, and target-selection studies generate both questions and answers for supplied targets. The fixed-example-allocation study instead generates answers to supplied questions, conditioned on two verified demonstrations while withholding the questions source answer (Appendix A.7). The learner minimizes supervised fine-tuning loss on incoming examples mixed with replay. The reference model stays frozen. Appendix C.3 gives the mixture objective, allocation weights, and study-specific controls. Evaluation separates new-task learning from preservation on replay and held-out tasks. Held-out examples, labels, descriptions, and scores are excluded from bank construction and target selection. Exploration protocols instead ask the model to propose new task descriptions, with or without access to the retained inventory, rather than select from the supplied entries. Appendix describes the generation interfaces, exploration procedures, and analysis-only comparison conditions.

sections.title: 3 Experiments
sections.content: We test how generated replay, bank composition, and target selection affect preservation beyond supplied targets and new-task learning. Held-out tasks are excluded from replay construction and target selection, so their results measure protection beyond the replay inventory.

sections.title: 3.1 Experimental Setting
sections.content: Models and benchmarks. We use Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-1.7B, and Qwen3-4B (Yang et al., 2025), with Qwen3.5-4B (Qwen Team, 2026) included in the forgetting diagnostics. Incoming tasks are MedQA (Jin et al., 2021) and CSTANCE from TRACE (Wang et al., 2023a). The Task Bank contains MMLU, HellaSwag, GSM8K, and BoolQ. ARC-Challenge (ARC-C), WinoGrande, PIQA, and SVAMP are held out from replay construction and target selection. Appendix gives study-specific model assignments, task roles, and evaluation formats. Training protocols. The endpoint, bank-composition, and target-selection studies use one epoch, learning rate of 1e-5, and five training seeds. Their MedQA comparisons use 1,024 incoming examples. Endpoint settings are selected during development and held fixed for evaluation, following Cha & Cho (2025). separate controlled forgetting sweep varies the model, incoming task, and learning rate {1e-7, 1e-6, 1e-5}, using one epoch of fullparameter AdamW. We also test fixed example allocation in which replay replaces incoming examples. That comparison controls nominal rows and update counts, while token exposure and generation cost can differ. Appendices A.3 and A.4 give optimizer settings, sweep grids, and study-specific allocations. Evaluation. We report incoming-task gains and prior-task accuracy changes in percentage points on the same pre/post evaluation examples. Where matched predictions are available, we also report Retention (correct correct): the percentage of initially correct answers that remain correct after the update, following Cho et al. (2026a). 3 This separates preserved answers from newly corrected errors. Error bars denote standard errors across training seeds. Appendix A.1 gives task aggregation and Retention eligibility rules.

sections.title: 3.2.1 Aggregate accuracy can conceal lost behavior
sections.content: Figure 1 shows incoming-task gains alongside prior-task losses. Within task, newly corrected answers can also offset the loss of previously correct answers (Harmon et al., 2025). Averaged over four held-out tasks and two seeds, 3.56% of examples become incorrect and 3.61% become correct, leaving only +0.05 pp net change (Figure 2). We therefore report paired Retention alongside task-level accuracy changes where matched predictions are available. Figure 2 Nearly unchanged accuracy can conceal substantial loss of previously correct answers. Leftward bars show correct-to-incorrect transitions. Rightward bars show incorrect-to-correct transitions. Diamonds show their net effect on accuracy. The four-task mean loses 3.56% and gains 3.61% of examples, for net +0.05 pp change. Qwen3-4B learns MedQA using 256 input rows, one epoch, 1e-6, and two seeds. Each task has 512 paired evaluation items. Bars use all items as the denominator. Retention (correct correct) conditions on initially correct items.

sections.title: 3.2.2 Broad replay improves preservation outside its inventory
sections.content: Broad replay protects held-out tasks more effectively than replay restricted to one target in the C-STANCE comparison (Figure 3). Mean held-out accuracy changes are 4.34 pp for SFT and 3.99 pp for Single-Task Replay, compared with +0.86 pp for Replay and +1.07 pp for Task-Bank Self-Replay. Incoming gains remain close, from +27.74 to +27.86 pp. Table 4 gives absolute scores. Figure 1 compares three model sizes on MedQA.

sections.title: 3.2.3 Combining supplied targets improves mean held-out Retention
sections.content: Combining the two supplied partial banks broadens the replay inventory and improves mean held-out Retention in all three tested models (Figure 4). The combined bank reaches 88.70%, 93.28%, and 96.01% Retention, exceeding the better partial bank by 4.42, 3.32, and 2.99 pp at 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B. Incoming gains are 0.45, 0.60, and 0.28 pp below SFT. The best bank varies by held-out task, while the combined bank has the best mean. Combining supplied targets therefore improves protection beyond the bank without requiring the model to discover new tasks.

sections.title: 3.2.4 Incoming-task information can improve target selection
sections.content: When replay uses only two bank entries, incoming-task information improves target selection at 4B, but gives no corresponding advantage at the smaller tested sizes (Figure 5). At 4B, incoming-aware selection reaches 95.69% mean held-out Retention, compared with 92.94% for random selection and 93.42% for bank-only selection. Its incoming gain is 0.04 pp above random selection, and Retention is within 0.32 pp of the full bank while using two of its four targets. The Retention difference from random selection is 0.76 pp at 0.6B and approximately zero at 1.7B. The observed selection advantage is limited to the tested 4B configuration. Learner, selector, and replay-generator strength are not varied independently. Appendix C.6 describes the selection interfaces. Proposed additions to the inventory are examined separately in the bank-aware discovery pilot (Appendix C.5). SVAMP accuracy increases by about six points after the MedQA update and about one after the C-STANCE update. The effect is heterogeneous across the evaluated capabilities, rather than uniform shift. sections.title: 4 Related Work
sections.content: Forgetting and continual learning. Replay and interference-aware methods mitigate forgetting by rehearsing prior experience or controlling updates that would disrupt it (Sun et al., 2019; Riemer et al., 2019; Aljundi et al., 2019). MIR selects replay examples according to anticipated interference (Aljundi et al., 2019). Our selection study instead chooses task entries before generating replay. With abundant replay memory, the remaining challenges can shift toward plasticity and computational cost (Cho et al., 2026c). Evaluation beyond the incoming task reveals changes that aggregate performance can conceal. TRACE studies continual language-model adaptation across diverse tasks and evaluates general abilities and instruction following (Wang et al., 2023a). Large-scale post-training analyses separate losses of previously correct behavior from gains that offset them in aggregate performance (Harmon et al., 2025). We use these task-level and paired views to evaluate preservation beyond partial inventory of targets. Generated preservation evidence and task exploration. Models can supply preservation evidence when prior data are limited. LAMOL rehearses previous tasks with generated pseudo-examples (Sun et al., 2019). Self-Synthesized Rehearsal uses in-context demonstrations to synthesize instances, refines their outputs, and selects diverse rehearsal data (Huang et al., 2024). The Self-Replay study of Marek et al. (2026) examines self-generated replay and its interaction with capacity and optimization. CPLUS uses anchor and self-probe gradients to regulate updates and demonstrates preservation beyond the supplied anchor task (Cho et al., 2026a). Our focus is how the organization of supplied targets affects the protection from generated replay. Generating candidate tasks raises separate question about what to preserve. Self-Instruct generates instructions and inputoutput examples for instruction tuning (Wang et al., 2023b), while Automated Capability Discovery proposes tasks to probe subject models capabilities (Lu et al., 2025). Task Banks provide an explicit inventory for studying the preservation value of task composition and selection. Our main comparisons use supplied targets. Model-proposed additions remain exploratory. Appendix extends these comparisons to task-free learning, on-policy supervision, and capability self-knowledge.

sections.title: 5 Discussion
sections.content: Toward sustained self-preservation. Our experiments leave open how to maintain useful inventory across successive updates. Proposed entries need demonstrated competence, distinct behavioral coverage, and incremental preservation value. Answering task correctly does not establish that the model can predict update damage or 9 choose effective replay. The single-arm expansion pilot produces negative accuracy changes. The two-update, one-seed pilot has mixed accuracy changes under prescribed task addition (Appendices C.5 and F). These findings motivate studying inventory revision alongside retention of capabilities learned across successive updates. Preservation under SFT. We study SFT because it is standard method for adapting pretrained models (Chen et al., 2024) and demanding setting for preservation. Comparisons with on-policy reinforcement learning and on-policy distillation report greater forgetting under SFT in the evaluated settings (Chen et al., 2026a; Shenfeld et al., 2026). Holding the update rule fixed lets us examine how replay source and target choice affect retention. On-policy training can reduce forgetting, but some degradation can remain (Shenfeld et al., 2026). Its different learning signals may also change which preservation targets are useful. The same evaluation of held-out retention and new-task learning therefore remains relevant across training regimes. Further discussion regarding target choice, scope, and cost analysis appears in Appendix G.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We study self-preservation of language models: how they can use their own knowledge to retain prior capabilities while learning new tasks. Task Banks provide simple way to examine preservation from an incomplete inventory of targets. Generated replay reduces forgetting beyond the bank, and combining partial banks improves mean held-out Retention. Selection informed by the incoming task further helps in the tested 4B setting, with similar new-task gains, but shows no corresponding advantage at smaller sizes. These benefits require evaluation of both retained behavior and new-task learning: average accuracy can conceal lost correct answers, and replay can reduce new-task gains when it replaces incoming examples. Language models can thus support broader preservation through generated data and, in some settings, useful choices about what to replay.

sections.content: A.1 Capability changes and loss of previously correct answers Capability changes compare post-update accuracy with the pre-update model on the same evaluation examples. We denote incoming-task gain by new and prior-task change by j, both in percentage points. We report individual tasks and equally weighted task groups, with standard errors across training seeds where available. We distinguish the minimum of capability means from the average of seed-wise minima: the former summarizes the average profile, while the latter asks how bad the worst capability is within each run. Table 1, Figure 6, and Table 8 average the worst held-out change within each seed. The five-seed endpoint profiles in Figures 3 and 12 instead take the minimum of task means. Paired seed-level uncertainty cannot be reconstructed from the supplied endpoint aggregates. Forgetting among initially correct examples measures different event: losing an answer that the pre-update model previously got right. Let θ0 and θ1 denote the pre-update and post-update model parameters. For evaluation task j, Fj = {i : fθ (xi) = yi, {i : fθ0 fθ1 (xi) = yi} (xi) = yi} . (1) Retention (correct correct) is the complement of Fj, expressed as percentage. This quantity cannot be recovered from pre/post accuracy alone because newly correct answers may offset previously correct answers that are lost. The same paired predictions explain how gains and losses can cancel in net accuracy, following the sample-wise view of Harmon et al. (2025). If Gj is the number of previously incorrect answers that become correct, Lj the number of previously correct answers lost, and Nj the evaluation size, then = 100(Gj Lj)/Nj. Figure 2 plots 100Gj/Nj and 100Lj/Nj from the recorded paired counts, using the same four held-out tasks for every summary. We report raw behavioral transitions, not the chance-adjusted quantities also developed by Harmon et al. (2025). They do not by themselves establish erasure of underlying knowledge. Conditioning on initially correct answers gives Fj different interpretation: the fraction of previously correct behavior lost, rather than the fraction of the full evaluation set that changes from correct to incorrect. The fixedexample-allocation comparison in Table 8 averages Fj over the eligible ARC-C, WinoGrande, and PIQA tasks. SVAMP does not meet the minimum number of initially correct examples. sections.title: B Additional Related Work
sections.content: Continual learning with structured interfaces. Continual learning can use explicit concepts to preserve interpretable predictions during adaptation. Tree of Concepts uses shallow decision tree to define fixed concept interface and updates the concept extractor and prediction head under clinical distribution shift (Cho et al., 2026b). Here, Task Banks provide an interface for specifying replay targets, and we evaluate whether their protection extends to held-out behaviors. Unsupervised and task-free continual learning. An incomplete preservation inventory is compatible with fully supervised incoming-task learning. Self-supervised continual learning learns representations from sequences of unlabeled inputs (Yang et al., 2023). Task-free and task-agnostic methods remove explicit task definitions or boundaries from the incoming stream (Wang et al., 2022; Ardywibowo et al., 2022). Our incoming data remain labeled and their task boundary known. The limited information concerns prior capabilities and differs by replay interface. Replay uses stored examples and labels. Task-Bank Self-Replay generates answers to supplied questions in the fixed-allocation study, and generates both questions and answers in the endpoint, bank-composition, and target-selection studies. Self-generated and on-policy supervision. Self-generated data can supply learning signals without separately labeled answer for every generated example. Self-Instruct generates instructions, inputs, and outputs, then filters invalid or 15 redundant examples before fine-tuning (Wang et al., 2023b). LAMOL uses generated pseudo-examples to rehearse earlier tasks (Sun et al., 2019). Even filtered model-generated examples can contain errors (Wang et al., 2023b). Their value for replay depends on whether they preserve earlier behavior while reducing dependence on stored examples (Marek et al., 2026). Self-generated supervision also supports adaptation through model-derived teachers and learning signals. Language models bootstrap from high-confidence solutions on unlabeled prompts (Huang et al., 2022), and self-play fine-tuning contrasts model-generated responses with demonstrations (Chen et al., 2024). Related methods use demonstration-conditioned or current-policy teachers (Shenfeld et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026b), model-generated update directives (Zweiger et al., 2025), or synthetic dreaming curricula (Behrouz et al., 2026). We use task descriptions and examples to guide replay generation, then study supplied-bank composition and target selection for an incoming update. Held-out evaluation tests whether this replay benefits behavior outside the supplied targets. Our exploratory bank-expansion pilot separately examines model-proposed additions. Task generation, capability discovery, and preservation breadth. Research on model-generated tasks extends beyond replay within single supplied target. Self-Instruct generates diverse instructions and their inputoutput examples for instruction tuning (Wang et al., 2023b). Automated Capability Discovery uses scientist model to propose tasks and probe subject model, including itself. Its objective is to discover and measure capabilities rather than protect them during an update (Lu et al., 2025). Absolute Zero learns task-proposal and solution curriculum with code-execution rewards to improve reasoning (Zhao et al., 2025). SEAL generates data and update directives for adaptation (Zweiger et al., 2025). These directions motivate model-generated inventories and learning signals, but task diversity or discovery alone does not establish preservation of prior correct behavior after fine-tuning. Prior preservation methods can also benefit tasks beyond their supplied examples. CPLUS uses self-probe gradients to limit interference and evaluates protection on benchmarks not represented in training (Cho et al., 2026a). Our focus is how partial preservation inventory can organize model-generated evidence to protect broader range of prior behavior. We study replay across supplied targets, combinations of banks, and selection of entries for an incoming update. The bank-expansion pilot provides an initial investigation of model-proposed additions, but establishing their preservation value relative to additional replay within the existing inventory remains an open question. Capability self-knowledge. Evidence about competence and update interference can inform self-preservation without implying privileged introspection. Language models can sometimes predict whether their own answers are correct, although calibration weakens under distribution shift (Kadavath et al., 2022). Our auxiliary diagnostics compare confidence-based competence estimates with measured task accuracy. Preservation is evaluated separately after the update. Estimating present competence and predicting which capabilities an update will harm are distinct questions.

sections.title: C Task Bank Interfaces and Auxiliary Diagnostics
sections.content: Replay interface Supplied to the model Model contributes Replay Supplied-question answers Question-and-answer generation Exploratory expanded bank Replay questions and labels Demonstrations and unlabeled questions Supplied task entries No generated replay answer Answers to supplied questions Replay questions and answers Incomplete task inventory Additional task entries, then questions and answers Table 6 Replay designs differ in the preservation information they require. These are alternative interfaces. The endpoint and supplied-bank composition/selection studies generate both questions and answers. The fixedexample-allocation study instead generates answers to supplied questions. Model-proposed additions are examined in the separate exploratory bank-expansion pilot. C.1 Prior capabilities, Task Banks, and held-out evaluation We formalize the prior capabilities that self-preservation aims to retain. Let denote the subset of the models preupdate capabilities whose performance should survive the update. common continual-learning setting exposes through named tasks or representative data. Our setting assumes that no exhaustive enumeration is available. 16 The Task Bank represents part of through task descriptions and examples, without claiming to enumerate it. We represent bank entry by bj = (dj, Ej, Uj): textual description dj, small demonstration set Ej, and an optional source of unlabeled prompts Uj. fixed bank = {b1, . . . , bm} defines the accessible replay inventory. An entry may support overlapping skills rather than certify distinct capability. The frozen reference model supplies replay through two generation interfaces. It either answers supplied prompts conditioned on demonstrations, or generates both questions and answers from task descriptions. These interfaces differ in how many questions, answers, and task descriptions are externally supplied  (Table 6)  . held-out evaluation tests whether the bank supports preservation beyond its own entries. Let = {Cm+1, . . . , Cm+r} denote the evaluation tasks excluded from bank construction and replay selection. method may not use held-out examples, reference answers, task descriptions, or scores to steer these decisions. This access boundary is distinct from the study-specific hyperparameter procedures in Appendix A.4. An independently proposed task may overlap capability measured by the held-out evaluation without receiving its data. Performance on tests whether bank-generated replay reduces forgetting. It does not by itself establish complete inventory of the models capabilities. C.2 Estimating competence from pre-update predictions As an auxiliary diagnostic, we test whether likelihoods from the pre-update model reveal its current competence. The seven multiple-choice tasks are ARC-C, BoolQ, C-STANCE, HellaSwag, MMLU, PIQA, and WinoGrande. These diagnostics are not used to select replay targets. For multiple-choice item with candidate sequence losses ℓi1, . . . , ℓiq, choice confidence is ci = max exp(ℓik) k=1 exp(ℓik ) . (2) We compare these confidence scores with observed correctness. At the item level, AUROC measures discrimination between correct and incorrect answers, Brier score measures probabilistic prediction error, and expected calibration error (ECE) measures calibration. At the task level, Spearman correlation and absolute calibration gap compare mean confidence with measured accuracy. limited probe budget gives an approximate estimate of task competence. For budget n, we sample labeled examples from capability and estimate accuracy by the mean correctness of the models predictions on those examples. We measure absolute error against accuracy on the disjoint remainder and repeat the split 100 times to estimate error at each probe budget. C.3 Replay mixture and fixed-example allocation The training mixture allocates examples between incoming data and selected replay entries. Given selected entry indices {1, . . . , m}, it is Dmix = (1 ρ) Dnew + ρ jS wjRj, jS wj = 1, (3) where Dnew and Rj are the empirical distributions of incoming examples and replay for entry j, ρ is the nominal replay fraction, and wj is each selected entrys share of replay. The learner minimizes LSFT(θ; Dmix) with respect to its parameters θ, while the reference model remains frozen. These weights describe example allocation. Tokenization, supervised token positions, and loss normalization determine the contribution to the training loss. Allocation and optimization settings are study-specific. At fixed nominal input allocation, replay replaces some new-task examples. The fixed-allocation study uses ρ = 59/256 before tokenization (59 replay rows and 197 new-task rows), while keeping the optimizer-step count fixed. The reported comparison includes SFT, random single-task replay, Replay, Task-Bank Self-Replay, and the post-hoc selector. Replay arms share the same nominal row allocation, initialization, learning rate, seeds, and update count. Token exposure and replay-generation overhead are not matched. The post-hoc selector provides an analysis-only reference for sparse replay. It ranks replay tasks by realized SFT damage and selects the most damaged task. Its access to post-update damage distinguishes it from selection rule available before training. It does not guarantee maximal replay benefit. Task-Bank Self-Replay changes the replay answers while keeping this allocation fixed. It uses the demonstrationconditioned procedure in Appendix A.7, with generation completed before training and held-out information excluded. This comparison tests generated answers to supplied questions, not newly invented questions or task entries. 17 C.4 Criteria for interpreting target discovery Useful proposals require distinct behavior, demonstrated competence, and added preservation value. Distinct behavior. different name or description does not certify new coverage. Structural validity and exact duplicate filtering do not detect all semantic overlap, including overlap between separate proposals. coverage audit must compare the proposed behaviors with both the initial inventory and the other additions, using independent behavioral probes and criteria fixed before post-update evaluation. Model explanations are candidate rationales, and do not certify novelty. Pre-update competence and faithful replay. The frozen model must demonstrate the proposed behavior on independent examples. self-reported ability or calibrated confidence is insufficient. Generated instances must elicit the behavior claimed by the entry: recognizing correct code fragment is not equivalent to writing code that passes tests. The current four-option generator supplies restricted recognition format. Without behavior-specific validation, its results cannot certify preservation of arbitrary generative or interactive skills. Incremental preservation value. Distinct, answerable tasks can still provide redundant or inefficient replay. causal interpretation requires the same adapted model and replay generator, with bank-aware additions compared against equal-budget replay generation within the partial bank and unguided additions. Incoming examples and order, update counts, loss weighting, replay tokens, and seeds must be controlled or their differences disclosed. Evaluation tasks remain sealed from proposal selection and generation. The relevant outcomes are Retention (correct correct), incoming-task gain, per-task changes, and paired uncertainty. single operating point does not establish an acquisitionretention frontier. Comparable protection with less learning is not evidence of better target selection. C.5 Negative bank-aware expansion pilot The bank-aware expansion pilot loses accuracy on the incoming task and all four held-out tasks. This Qwen3-1.7B seed-1 pilot adapts the model to MedQA with 1,024 incoming examples and 256 generated replay examples, learning rate 1e-5, and 80 optimizer updates. It uses the bank-aware expanded inventory with an availabilitybalanced development replay pool. sections.title: F Sequential Preservation Pilot

sections.title: G Further Discussion and Limitations
sections.content: Choosing preservation targets. Preservation depends on which targets supply replay and how their examples are generated. Combining partial banks improves mean held-out Retention, and incoming-aware selection helps at the tested 4B operating point (Figures 4 and 5). Assessing these benefits requires new-task gains, individual-task changes, and Retention on tasks excluded from replay. Scope. The experiments establish preservation behavior only within the reported models, tasks, and short update sequences. They cover Qwen checkpoints, two incoming tasks, and eight prior benchmark capabilities, including four held-out evaluation tasks. Transfer to that held-out evaluation does not establish preservation of the full pretrained repertoire, and stable low baseline performance can provide little evidence of retained competence. Most studies concern one update. The two-stage, one-seed pilot has mixed outcomes and does not establish sustained autonomous preservation. Controls and cost. The experimental controls limit causal and uncertainty claims. Selected model comparisons vary learning rate and model generation, so they do not isolate scaling effect. Two-seed controlled studies and five-seed endpoint aggregates limit uncertainty analysis. The latter do not support paired significance tests or within-update trajectories. Under fixed example allocation, improved preservation accompanies smaller new-task gains as replay replaces incoming examples. This study matches nominal input rows and optimizer steps, while tokenized exposure and generation overhead differ. These distinctions prevent treating every cross-study contrast as controlled comparison of single factor. Targets and supervision. Task-Bank Self-Replay depends on supplied preservation targets. It reduces some supervision requirements without eliminating them or certifying autonomous discovery. Replay can reproduce model errors, and supplied-question replay still relies on verified demonstrations. The bank-aware discovery pilot does not establish whether new proposed targets improve preservation over fixed partial bank. The evidence does not establish robustness across independent task omissions, prompt variants, or alternative task-addition rules.
